/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.headline: Prisoners thank Andy Burnham as they leave jail in first wave of early releases
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.excerpt: Prisoners have thanked Andy Burnham as they celebrated walking free from jail early. The first wave of releases began on Thursday, with 700 offenders walking out across England and Wales under the government’s plan to ease prison overcrowding. Those released from dozens of prisons under the government’s latest early release scheme on Thursday were greeted by huddles of journalists requesting their personal messages for the prime minister. Some offenders said they would soon return to jail, because they had nowhere to live and would breach their licence conditions. It follows the damaging early release scheme under Keir Starmer in 2024 when offenders were photographed holding bottles of champagne while saying: “Big up Starmer”. Among the first releases, a former bus driver turned shoplifter, Michael Bogle, 38, from Brent, north London, stepped into the sunlight outside HMP Wandsworth, a south London prison notable for a string of recent scandals. Having served 78 days in prison after breaching a 32-week suspended sentence for shoplifting, he was released early and was pleased that he had been given a place in a bail hostel in south-east London. Asked for his message to Burnham, he said: “Keep the early release going. It’s good.” Bogle, who has been jailed five separate times for 100 convictions, said he had been driven to shoplift “so he could eat” after being made homeless. Prison was “terrible”, Bogle said, adding that there were “too many drugs”.
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.trail: Seven hundred offenders from dozens of prisons in England and Wales expected to be freed on Thursday

/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.headline: Prisoners freed early in England and Wales risk living on the streets, say probation officers
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.excerpt: Hundreds of prisoners are due to be released early from jail on Thursday amid warnings that many will have nowhere to live and the probation system will struggle to monitor them. About 2,000 criminals including domestic abusers and violent offenders are to be freed over the next month, with another 3,000 in stages over the next year to ease overcrowding. The number was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by the prime minister, Andy Burnham. Prisoners are supposed to be found appropriate accommodation before their release, significantly reducing reoffending rates. But a probation source told the Guardian that their colleagues in some towns and cities were struggling to find hostel places. “We have a handful of places for ex-offenders and they are full. We are now looking at releasing some people straight on to the street,” the source said. Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said: “We know that leaving prison homeless can put people on a path back into custody. It is vital that the whole system from prisons and probation to councils and community providers work together to give people a roof over their heads.” Napo, the probation officers’ union, has raised the issue of the accommodation shortage with prison bosses. The task of finding beds for prisoners is expected to reach critical levels from 13 October, when a second tranche of prisoners is due for release.
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.trail: Warning of a lack of hostel places for 2,000 criminals due to be released over the next month to ease overcrowding

/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.headline: More sex offenders in England and Wales could be released amid court system crisis, police sources say
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.excerpt: More sexual predators in England and Wales could be freed instead of jailed because of the pressure on courts and prisons, police sources have told the Guardian. The warning comes after the Metropolitan police commissioner, Mark Rowley, on Thursday condemned the release on bail of a man after he admitted taking pictures of children and women, and then using AI to sexualise them. Zafer Dogan was bailed to his flat overlooking a children’s playground, from which he committed some of the offences he admitted, despite prosecutors and police saying he should be remanded in custody. One of his victims said they had to move after courts declined to send him to jail ahead of his sentencing on Thursday, where he was imprisoned for two years. A senior police source said they feared more such cases across England and Wales, where charged suspects are released rather than jailed: “We are bracing ourselves for more of this across the country, that is, offenders who should be remanded, instead being freed on bail, to the distress of their victims. “Some forces are better resourced to deal with this than others. It is going to be a nationwide issue.” The government’s early release policy, to ease pressure on prisons where places are on the verge of running out, is expected to start next Thursday. The police source added: “Probation is crumbling, policing is having to pick up extra offender management work which it has not had to do before. Something has got to give.
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.trail: Sources tell the Guardian they are braced for more offenders being bailed into the community ahead of October’s early prisoner release

/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.headline: Hope for UK mothers accused of child abduction after fleeing domestic violence
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.excerpt: British mothers who bring their children with them when returning to the UK after fleeing from domestic abuse abroad – which can lead to them being accused of abduction – could be given greater legal protection and support. The government has agreed to examine how domestic abuse features in international child abduction cases, with a view to giving survivors of domestic abuse more help fighting partners’ demands that they return children to their home countries. The changes would come too late for Claire, who lived in the US with an abusive partner and their two small children for more than a decade. But they could help mothers like her. “We were all terrified of him. I was in near-constant fear for my life,” she said. “Eventually, I escaped and got us all on a plane back home to the UK.” She lived in hiding for three months, but eventually had to apply for benefits. “Within a day, the police were at our door with summons under the Hague convention to appear in court just nine days later,” she said. Approximately 500 Hague-convention applications for the return of a child are filed each year in England and Wales. Between 10% and 20% of children affected end up being separated from their primary carer owing to a formal court-ordered return. Claire was fortunate: she used all of her savings to instruct a barrister, and her children were able to stay in the UK.
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.trail: Women escaping abusive partners abroad could get new protections from legal analysis of Hague convention

/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.headline: Specialist courtrooms to prioritise rape cases in England and Wales
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.excerpt: Specialist courtrooms prioritising cases of rape and other serious sex offences are to be introduced across England and Wales, with campaigners welcoming the move as potentially transformative. The changes, designed to encourage more survivors to come forward, will include the provision of private entrances and waiting rooms, and facilities equipped for recording evidence in advance and observing sentencing remotely. Announcing the move, Andy Burnham said victims of rape and serious sexual offences had felt let down by the justice system for too long, adding that prosecution rates for rape remained “shamefully low”, with many victims waiting years for justice. “These changes are long overdue and will make a significant difference, but focusing on prosecution alone will not be enough,” the prime minister said. “So as well as ensuring victims get justice, we will step up action to prevent these horrific crimes from happening in the first place.” A multimillion-pound cash injection is intended to make sure every crown court in England and Wales has at least one room set up specifically to hear rape and serious sexual offence cases within two years. Rape and serious sexual offence cases will also be prioritised in courts more widely, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) announced. Such trials will be given a fixed date, as opposed to being placed on floating lists where they can be moved at short notice and delayed by months.
/law/2026/oct/04/ministers-drop-radical-.trail: Funding boost for facilities and fixed dates for trials designed to encourage more survivors to come forward

/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.headline: OpenAI’s Medicare attack has exposed Australia’s ‘tech debt’. Fixing it could bring a big bill for taxpayers
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.excerpt: The Australian government faces significant “tech debt” that could bring a big bill for taxpayers after the OpenAI Medicare breach, as government agencies will need to fortify their defences against future attacks by AI agents. This week, the home affairs department ordered all federal government agencies to conduct a “legacy technology stocktake” that requires a plan for each agency to “reduce legacy technology systems” to a level within the agency’s risk tolerance and appetite, the direction stated. OpenAI this week revealed an internal agent had gained non-public access to the Services Australia Medicare statistics portal during a training task seeking information on government spending on skin conditions in Victoria. The agent was able to run commands, retrieve internal files, credentials, and write files. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email While OpenAI has apologised to Australia for the incident, it has served as a wake up call for the federal government, with the government-wide review now under way. The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, asked her department whether some of the A$160m funding allocated to the agency in the last budget for cyber upgrades can be accelerated. The statistics portal, Gallagher told reporters last month, is a “legacy system.” “It dates back decades.” Services Australia will be far from alone in managing legacy systems.
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.trail: Home affairs department orders all federal government agencies to conduct review of ‘legacy technology’ amid fallout from AI agent hacks

/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.headline: AI chatbots remove hijabs from images of Muslim women when prompted
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.excerpt: When prompted, AI chatbots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith. The Guardian asked ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini and Claude to take the veil off an AI-generated image of a woman wearing a hijab. Both OpenAI’s ChatGPT and xAI’s Grok bots complied with the prompt. Anthropic’s Claude responded that it does not have an image-editing or -generating feature but that it would not alter a photo to remove someone’s hijab. Gemini initially said that it could not remove clothing or head coverings from photos of real people because it could not digitally alter someone’s appearance without their consent. But when asked to make the woman look more “western”, the bot created an image of her without her hijab. The Guardian US tested the chatbots after a French far-right politician stripped a real Muslim woman of her hijab and long-sleeved dress in a picture he made clear was modified. Julien Odoul, a member of parliament and of the National Rally party, posted the altered image of the woman on X with her hair visible and arms exposed alongside the caption “LIBERTÉ FRANÇAISE”, meaning French Liberty. He quote-tweeted the original image, posted by someone else, which showed the woman crossing a street wearing a hijab and full-length dress.
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.trail: Guardian tested chatbots after French far-right politician stripped a Muslim woman of her hijab in a photo

/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.headline: Trump AI deal rebrands ‘artificial intelligence’ as ‘superintelligence’
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.excerpt: Donald Trump announced on Tuesday that the heads of the largest US tech and AI companies had signed a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. He announced the deal, called the Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities, following a White House luncheon with top tech executives. “It’s almost like a constitution in a way, and the biggest people in the world signed that, and I signed it as president, and it really ⁠is a form of protection,” Trump said. Trump also signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “superintelligence”, similar to a declaration he made at the United Nations last week. “The Order directs all departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and non-statutory documents within the executive branch and to no longer acknowledge the terms ‘Artificial Intelligence’ or ‘AI’,” the order declared. The agreement, which Trump suggested would allow the companies to perform “tremendous self-policing” of their products and technologies, outlines a vague framework for how AI firms would establish safety standards as they test out new products. The tech industry has faced increased public scrutiny following a series of incidents in which major AI companies’ products hacked into outside organizations during safety tests.
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.trail: The US president announces vague ‘morally binding’ AI agreement among tech CEOs for ‘tremendous self-policing’

/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.headline: OpenAI announces ‘dots’ agent after scrapping launch of new AI model over safety concerns
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.excerpt: Less than 24 hours after OpenAI announced it would scrap the launch of an artificial intelligence model over safety concerns, the company debuted a whole new suite of AI tools. During its annual showcase for developers in San Francisco on Tuesday, Sam Altman, OpenAI’s CEO, enthusiastically unveiled an AI agent called “dots” that he said was “more ambitious” than ChatGPT and a “whole new way to work with AI”. “It’s like an AI helper that always has your back,” Altman said, to loud applause from the developers attending the event. “In the future, if you like, you can work with a whole team of dots.” OpenAI’s dots are colorful little blobs, donning berets or glasses, that appear on people’s phones or laptops, can be integrated into other apps and can follow commands. The agents can perform tasks without supervision such as schedule a meeting, book a flight or dole out assignments to colleagues. OpenAI says the “dots are an extension of you” and describes the tool as “frontier intelligence”. Dots are powered by GPT-6 Astra, the company’s latest model. OpenAI said the previous evening it would halt the release of GPT-6.1 Astra because the updated model showed deceptive behavior during testing. OpenAI’s dots will compete with Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released two weeks ago. Meta’s product is aimed at everyday consumers more than business customers, as OpenAI’s is, though Meta announced a small business offering on Tuesday.
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.trail: Company’s product comes weeks after Meta introduced its own artificial intelligence agent Muse

/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.headline: The AI agents are spiraling out of control
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.excerpt: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you as rain and wind lash my windows in New York City. Today in tech, we’re discussing an alarming series of disclosures by AI companies. AI agents spiral out of control just as they go mainstream The agents are spiraling out of control. Their makers can’t rein them in. And yet everyone is getting one. Since Friday, OpenAI has made a series of disclosures that have widened the scope of its AI agents’ rogue activity considerably and concerningly. In addition to hacking the developer forum Hugging Face, which was disclosed in July, the company revealed its bots broke into Australia’s government healthcare system; meddled in US government websites for the departments of education and commerce; leaked more than 50 images from ChatGPT users; and “bruteforced” a United Nations website that blocked them from accessing data. Though these incidents are severe each on their own, they seem to represent only a small sample. Both OpenAI and Anthropic are investigating tens of thousands of incidents of problematic behavior by their frontier models, per Axios. Sam Altman said OpenAI was sifting through “petabytes of agent activity logs”. (A petabyte of data would fill thousands of average laptops.) In response to the major errors, OpenAI has paused the training of its latest models. Be skeptical of this declaration. The company made a similar announcement in August.
/technology/2026/oct/03/openai-safety-le.trail: As OpenAI discloses multiple incidents of its technology going rogue and the UN warns of uncontrollable agents, Meta is putting an AI agent in the hands of millions

/politics/2026/oct/03/andy-burnham-confe.headline: Wednesday briefing: ​Can Andy Burnham live up to the party’s faith in him?
/politics/2026/oct/03/andy-burnham-confe.excerpt: Good morning from Liverpool (and hello again to the newsletter subscribers I met in person, as I took First Edition on tour to Labour party conference). It’s the first gathering of the party faithful since Andy Burnham ousted Keir Starmer in July, in what I’ve heard delicately referred to as a “soft coup”, and the theme of this conference is “Hope again.” Yesterday, in an engaging and emotional speech that staked out bold positions on some of the most intractable issues of the day – social care, NEETs, electoral reform, the EU – Burnham added substance to the slogan that graces the banners hanging from the lofty ceilings of the exhibition hall. You can read our politics team’s key takeaways here. Meanwhile, on the conference fringe yesterday evening, the debate continued between energised activists and “policy grownups” warning of dire fiscal headwinds. Five big stories UK news | One of the five men arrested near RAF Fairford as part of a terror investigation that prompted fears of an Iran-backed plot called the police to report the incident. /politics/2026/oct/03/andy-burnham-confe.headline: Burnham gambles on radical progressive plan to help Britain ‘rise again’
/politics/2026/oct/03/andy-burnham-confe.excerpt: Andy Burnham has staked his future on a gamble that the public will back radical progressive policies on social care, electoral reform and Europe, telling voters that his agenda will break the mould of the last 40 years and “allow us to rise again”. In a deeply personal speech at Labour’s conference, Burnham began building his next general election manifesto, acknowledging that he may end up paying the price for creating sharp new dividing lines in politics. “I won’t pretend some of this won’t be difficult,” he said. “I accept I may pay a political price. But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.” However, while the prime minister said he would try to give people some “breathing space” on the cost of living, he admitted his ambitious policy prospectus would have to wait until after the next election because of the state of the public finances. “These things are not everything, but I hope you will see it as a sign – a strong one – of our intent to get your bills and fares down as you wait for the bigger changes to come,” he told Labour activists. “I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford. I will stick to our fiscal rules to get borrowing and debt down.

/politics/2026/oct/03/andy-burnham-confe.headline: Andy Burnham expected to say he will push ahead with electoral reform plans
/politics/2026/oct/03/andy-burnham-confe.excerpt: Andy Burnham is expected to announce that he will push ahead with plans for electoral reform in his first conference speech as Labour leader, in the latest sign that he intends to radically transform the UK’s political system. The prime minister, a longtime advocate of reform, will kick off a process that could eventually lead to ditching the first-past-the-post system in favour of proportional representation. Government sources told the Guardian that Burnham would set out his plans in “broad strokes” in the speech, underlining his commitment to drawing up proposals before the next general election. Along with social care changes and closer ties with the EU, the plans – which would represent the most significant shake-up of the electoral system since 1918 – would then be put in Labour’s manifesto to get public backing. One option open to Burnham is to set up a new national commission for electoral reform, an idea he endorsed at last year’s party conference as Greater Manchester mayor. At the time, he said there should be “a manifesto commitment to a system of proportional representation to be introduced into Westminster elections in the next parliament”. Almost 100 Labour MPs supported the plan when the representation of the people bill went through parliament earlier this month. The minister leading the bill, Florence Eshalomi, told MPs that Burnham “remains committed to electoral reform”, while warning it was “premature to legislate now for one approach”.
/politics/2026/oct/03/andy-burnham-confe.trail: Exclusive: Labour conference speech will kick off process that could replace current system with proportional representation

/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.headline: Trial of live facial recognition in London stations leads to a false positive and no arrests
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.excerpt: A six-month trial of live facial recognition (LFR) technology in London’s railway stations that cost more than £320,000 and almost 100 hours of police officers’ time led to one false match against a watchlist of suspects and no arrests. More than half a million faces were scanned between February and July this year in some of the capital’s busiest transport hubs during the British Transport Police (BTP) trial of the surveillance technology, which aimed to help catch offenders and people breaching court orders. A freedom of information document obtained by Liberty Investigates and shared with the Guardian shows that equipment hire and police staffing for the 18 deployments across the trial cost £320,786 and led to only one alert on a watchlist, which turned out to be an incorrect identification, also known as a false positive. Last month BTP announced it was extending the trial for a further four months and expanding the deployments to include London Underground stations. British Transport Police said that since the extension there had been three positive confirmed alerts of people who were subsequently confirmed to be complying with sexual harm prevention orders or other imposed court conditions.
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.trail: Freedom of information request finds six-month trial cost £320,000, used almost 100 police hours and led to just one – incorrect – alert

/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.headline: Court quashes 1976 theft convictions over link to corrupt London police officer
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.excerpt: Two men have had theft convictions quashed at the court of appeal half a century after they were wrongfully arrested because of a corrupt police officer, although one did not live to see his exoneration. Christopher Poulter and Kevin Biggs were 21 and 18 respectively when they were convicted in 1976 of taking 13 mailbags from a wagon in a Clapham goods yard in London. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) referred their case to the court of appeal this year after new evidence emerged about the disgraced police officer DS Derek Ridgewell. Ridgewell was jailed for seven years in 1980 after stealing more than £1m in goods, and was found to have framed innocent young black men for his own crimes, the CCRC said. He was one of three officers said to have seen Poulter and Biggs taking the mailbags and fleeing by car. The men’s defence was that they had been in a pub in Tooting, south London, all night, before being approached by officers and arrested. Poulter was sentenced to a year in prison and Biggs was sentenced to training at a borstal, or young offenders’ institution, at their hearing at inner London crown court 50 years ago. The innocence of Biggs, who died in 2004, emerged through an investigation by the British Transport Police, who were searching for victims of Ridgewell. He and Poulter are the 14th and 15th people to have had their convictions quashed in relation to Ridgewell’s misconduct.
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.trail: Christopher Poulter and Kevin Biggs, who died in 2004, exonerated of mailbag theft after new evidence emerged

/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.headline: ‘Just cut the wires’: why UK conspiracy theorists are destroying traffic scanners
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.excerpt: At the top of an extendable ladder on a quiet street of Ilfracombe, in Devon, an older woman dressed smartly in cropped trousers, a red rain jacket and matching red socks is chopping at some wires at the top of a set of traffic lights with a small pair of pliers. A grey-haired man holding a takeaway coffee supports the ladder, while others, filming their activities, give encouragement from behind the camera. “Yeah, that’s how you do it,” says one man. “Just cut the wires.” Posted to social media after the incident on 28 August, the footage rapidly attracted attention. To some, it was an act of straightforward vandalism; a woman in her 60s and man in his 70s were later arrested and bailed on suspicion of criminal damage and causing danger to road users. Others, however, believed the woman should be lauded. “Not all heroes wear capes,” reads one Facebook comment on a supporter’s page. “Bideford and Barnstaple next, please,” reads another. Most people view traffic lights as helpful landmarks that keep road and pavement users safe. To a group who call themselves “Blade Runners”, however, the traffic scanners installed above them increasingly conceal a sinister purpose: to install “phased array electronic assault weapons” on city streets that they claim can carry out mass surveillance and even cause cancer, dementia and sudden death.
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.trail: Sensors that monitor vehicle volume are said to be ‘electronic assault weapons’ by the ‘Blade Runners’ group

/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.headline: Deep cuts: how one Londoner’s fake vinyl empire sheds light on ‘industrial scale’ fraud
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.excerpt: From 2017 onwards, Rehan Ahmed styled himself as a savvy business owner. But behind the facade of a successful entrepreneur lurked one stark fact: his empire was built on fakery. On Friday, the man behind the biggest-ever UK case of producing fraudulent vinyl, who sold counterfeit copies of records by some of the world’s biggest artists including Taylor Swift, Coldplay and Kendrick Lamar, was jailed. Ahmed, a 40-year-old father of three from Southall, west London, pleaded guilty to two charges of breach of artists’ copyright, and acquiring and using criminal property. On the first count, Judge Darren Reed sentenced him to two years and eight months in prison, while the more serious second charge led to a custodial penalty of three and a half years. The sentences will be served concurrently, meaning that the second will dictate the time Ahmed spends in prison. In a sentencing hearing at Inner London crown court on Friday, the judge highlighted the “sophisticated and planned nature of the enterprise”, and the fact that Ahmed had caused “wider harm to the music industry”. *** Operating under the company names Phoenix of Vinyl and Paragon Music, Ahmed produced counterfeit vinyl albums that he supplied to record shops or sold directly to consumers through online platforms such as Discogs and eBay. In 2025, eBay removed about 7.9m potentially counterfeit or prohibited items from the platform. A spokesperson said: “Counterfeits are strictly prohibited on eBay.
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.trail: Thousands of knock-off records worth a fortune are being seized in the UK by anti-counterfeit police stings

/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.headline: UK man admits using online network for sexual crimes against unconscious woman
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.excerpt: A man has admitted using an online sexual abuse network to commit a host of sexual crimes, along with another man, against the latter’s unconscious wife. Darren Conway, 52, pleaded guilty to 11 charges at Wood Green crown court. They included voyeurism, possession of extreme pornography and encouraging the other man to sexually abuse his wife on Conway’s behalf. “Conway’s actions were shocking,” said Scotland Yard’s Commander Andy Day. “By encouraging others to engage in sexual offending against victims who were unconscious, asleep, or otherwise stupefied, he has put women at a serious risk of harm in their own homes – all for his own sexual gratification.” Day said it was a case of “drug-facilitated sexual offending” that could have a “lasting and devastating impacts on its victims”. Conway solicited naked images of sleeping women on at least 10 occasions between 2023 and 2026, according to the indictment. While most of the charges to which he pleaded guilty on Friday related to the wife of the man with whom he was in contact, police fear there are many more victims. Officers said they were still working to identify others in footage found on Conway’s devices – adding that, “while much of the offending is believed to have taken place in the UK, it is also possible that some victims are based overseas”.
/uk-news/2026/oct/03/met-launches-inquir.trail: Darren Conway pleads guilty to voyeurism and encouraging a husband to abuse his wife

/football/2026/oct/03/croatia-england-na.headline: Pickford in spotlight against Croatia with England position under threat from Trafford
/football/2026/oct/03/croatia-england-na.excerpt: For England’s first meeting with Luka Modric you have to go back 20 years. Croatia were managed by Slaven Bilic, who has returned for a second spell in charge of the national team, and dominated in Zagreb. They eased to a 2-0 win, Steve McClaren’s doomed attempt to qualify for Euro 2008 took a turn for the worse and, as well as Modric giving England’s midfield the runaround, the game was remembered best for a horror mistake from the Three Lions No 1. Paul Robinson must have wanted the ground to swallow him up when he kicked at thin air and let Gary Neville’s backpass bobble into the net. Robinson, his aura diminished, never really recovered. The goalkeeper made 10 more appearances but after another crucial error against Russia in October 2007, he never won another cap. Goalkeepers live a fragile existence. Joe Hart experienced a sharp decline and Jordan Pickford is under real pressure for the first time since becoming No 1 just before the 2018 World Cup. James Trafford played the first two of England’s games in Nations League Group A3 and did well against Spain and Czechia. However, Pickford will return when England face Croatia and Modric in Rijeka on Saturday evening. Thomas Tuchel has divided the games. Pickford is due to continue when England close this camp by hosting Czechia on Tuesday. Tuchel’s explanation is that he wanted to test Trafford against elite opposition. He says Pickford has done nothing wrong.

/football/2026/oct/03/croatia-england-na.headline: Bilic is back: bravery and belief underpin second coming as Croatia manager
/football/2026/oct/03/croatia-england-na.excerpt: “I don’t believe in comebacks.” Slaven Bilic sat in the lobby of a hotel in Canary Wharf wearing a black Soundgarden T-shirt and dark denim, confidently discussing a wide variety of topics ranging from Sir Alex Ferguson’s autobiography to historical epics of Yugoslav cinematography and Nikola Tesla’s celibacy. He was living the good life in London, just before his third Premier League season as West Ham’s manager, and a rare interview for Croatian media was a chance for him to catch up with domestic intrigues. “I’m now distanced by default, geographically,” he said, breathing a sigh of relief, before continuing to jump from subject to subject; a bit about a Metallica concert, then a bit about steaks at an Argentinian restaurant, followed by some off-record anecdotes. He was clearly enjoying himself and didn’t hesitate to show it; his time as Croatia’s manager seemed long gone, although he always left a bittersweet aftertaste when talking about them. “I have nice memories and wouldn’t want to spoil them,” he said. “I don’t like coming back. It’s not the fear of failure, just the feeling that something has run its course.” And yet, here we are now. Nine years after that interview – and 14 since his first spell as Croatia’s manager ended – Bilic is back at the helm and preparing to face England in Rijeka in the Nations League on Saturday.
